title: Vowel Qualities and Vowel Letters
description: Compare pure-long, tone-long, and short vowels.

blocks.caption: Summary
blocks.html: Hebrew has three primary vowel qualities — a, i, and u — and two more, e and o. Each appears long or short. Length matters: a long vowel fills a syllable differently from a short one, and many noun and verb patterns depend on the difference. Learn the pairs — long ā and short a, long ē and short e, long î and short i, long ô and short o, long û and short u — and notice that the vowel letters ו and י usually accompany the long forms.

blocks.caption: Vowel length
blocks.html: A long vowel is often written with a vowel letter to hold it, while a short vowel usually stands alone. Compare קָטַל (qāṭal): the first vowel is long ā under ק, the second is short a under ט. The pattern of long and short vowels is part of the word's identity, so changing length often changes meaning or form.

blocks.caption: Qamets and qamets-hatuf
blocks.html: The sign qamets (ָ) usually stands for long ā, but in a closed, unaccented syllable it is read as short o, called qamets-hatuf. The difference is governed by the syllable, so it is best learned together with syllable division: a qamets in a closed syllable that is not stressed is the short o.

blocks.caption: Common confusion
blocks.html: Do not assume one sign always means one sound in every position. Qamets is the clearest example: ā in one syllable, o in another. When you meet a new word, divide it into syllables first, then decide how a qamets is read.
